query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, earlier studies separately examined tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes during cold rolling, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and hardening after aging at 600–800 °C. However, these findings do not provide a unified explanation of the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. Thermal expansion is also relevant because mismatch can produce thermal stresses during composite solidification and potentially affect strength. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the unresolved behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, observations predicted relative to a baseline, the relevant temperature and response boundaries, how the earlier findings support the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The unique stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior of the HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy is governed by temperature‐dependent local lattice distortions arising from thermal expansion mismatch among constituent elements. These distortions alter the elastic anisotropy and promote enhanced edge dislocation activity at elevated temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy with a single-phase BCC structure and inherent atomic-scale lattice distortions from compositional heterogeneity.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled thermal cycling under constant strain rate loading while performing in situ neutron diffraction measurements combined with theoretical elastic modulus modeling.
generation.conditions: Testing over a temperature range from room temperature (~293 K) up to ~1273 K, maintaining identical processing history for baseline and modified samples. A controlled comparison between as-cast (or homogenized) samples and samples pre-treated (e.g., cold rolled to enhance lattice distortions) is required.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions induced by thermal expansion mismatch among the constituent elements, which modulate elastic anisotropy and the activation of edge dislocation mechanisms.
generation.mechanism: Differential thermal expansion creates local elastic inhomogeneities that modify the diffraction elastic moduli and promote a shift toward edge dislocation-mediated plasticity at elevated temperatures, thereby unifying the observed stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline at room temperature, in situ neutron diffraction will reveal increased lattice strain heterogeneity and altered elastic moduli at elevated temperatures. Samples with enhanced lattice distortions (e.g., via cold rolling) will show a more pronounced change in dislocation character (increased edge dislocation activity) and a measurable shift in theoretical vs. experimental elastic moduli.
generation.baseline: Baseline samples with minimal induced lattice distortion, exhibiting relatively uniform elastic moduli and standard dislocation behavior at room temperature.
generation.boundary: Temperature range from ~293 K to ~1273 K under constant load/strain rate conditions; the influence of microstructural modifications is isolated by comparing homogenized versus pre-deformed samples.
generation.uncertainty: The relative magnitude of the effects caused by thermal expansion-induced lattice mismatch versus other factors (e.g., phase transformations or precipitation during aging) remains uncertain and will require detailed calibration and quantitative analysis.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr alloy samples: one set with a homogenized microstructure and another with induced lattice distortions via cold rolling. Subject both sets to thermal cycling from 293 K to 1273 K while applying constant strain rate tensile loading. Perform in situ neutron diffraction to measure changes in diffraction elastic moduli and analyze dislocation character using complementary microscopy techniques.
measurements: Diffraction elastic moduli as a function of temperature
Lattice strain distribution and its heterogeneity
Dislocation density and character (edge versus screw) via microscopy
Macroscopic stress–strain curves under controlled loading conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the induced microstructural differences do not produce significant changes in the temperature-dependent lattice strain heterogeneity, elastic moduli, or dislocation character compared to the homogenized samples, or if no correlation is found between thermal expansion mismatch and the observed mechanical behavior, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThe NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 is a refractory multi-principal-element alloy with high strength and good ductility at room temperature. It is important for possible high-temperature applications to investigate the deformation mechanism of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy at different temperatures using tensile tests. In this investigation, the tensile tests were conducted at room temperature to 1273 K on sheet materials fabricated by cold rolling combined with annealing treatments. At 473 K, the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy exhibited a high tensile ductility (12%). At a testing temperature range of 673~873 K, the ductility was reduced, but the yield strength remained above 800 MPa, which is rare in most other alloys. The TEM investigations revealed that a dislocation slip controlled the plastic deformation, and the degree of deformation was closely related to the dislocation density. The true stress–strain curves of the alloy under different deformation conditions were obtained by tensile deformation at different deformation temperatures (673~873 K) and strain rates (0.001~0.0005 s−1). The present work discovers the unique deformation behavior of a refractory high-entropy alloy at elevated temperatures. Single-phase solid-solution refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) show remarkable mechanical properties, such as their high yield strength and substantial softening resistance at elevated temperatures. Hence, the in-depth study of the deformation behavior for body-centered cubic (BCC) refractory HEAs is a critical issue to explore the uncovered/unique deformation mechanisms. We have investigated the elastic and plastic deformation behaviors of a single BCC NbTaTiV refractory HEA at elevated temperatures using integrated experimental efforts and theoretical calculations. The in situ neutron diffraction results reveal a temperature-dependent elastic anisotropic deformation behavior. The single-crystal elastic moduli and macroscopic Young’s, shear, and bulk moduli were determined from the in situ neutron diffraction, showing great agreement with first-principles calculations, machine learning, and resonant ultrasound spectroscopy results. cited_evidence.text: The observation of a high fraction of edge dislocations relative to screw dislocations is in distinct contrast to typical studies in BCC metals and other HEAs that almost exclusively show long straight screw dislocations and do not have good high-T strengths. While results from TEM and neutron diffraction are not quantitatively identical, both results consistently show that edge dislocations are prevalent and dominant, as compared to screws. Our experimental demonstration that plasticity in a BCC alloy can be controlled by edge dislocations is very surprising because it is counter to the nearly universally accepted understanding, based on many observations in elemental and dilute BCC alloys over many decades, that screw dislocations completely dominate the plastic-flow behavior,.
